questions.question: How do you do back-of-the-envelope estimation for system design? What numbers should you know?
questions.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation: Capacity Planning for System Design
questions.direct_answer: Start with user count and daily active users (DAU). Convert to requests/sec (DAU × actions/user ÷ 86,400 × peak multiplier). Then estimate storage (rows × row size × retention), bandwidth (requests × payload size), and cache size (working set × object size). Know the key latency numbers: L1 cache 1ns, RAM 100ns, SSD 100μs, HDD 10ms, same-datacenter round trip 0.5ms, cross-continent 150ms.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to quickly size a system and determine whether a design is feasible before diving into architecture
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting lost in precise math instead of using order-of-magnitude estimates — the goal is feasibility, not accuracy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the estimation framework systematically: QPS → storage → bandwidth → cache → number of servers. Use powers of 2 fluently.

sections.title: Why Estimation Comes Before Architecture
sections.content:
Before drawing a single box on a whiteboard, you need to know the **order of magnitude** of the system you're designing. Is it handling 100 requests/second or 100,000? Does it store 1 GB or 1 PB? The answer determines whether you need a single PostgreSQL instance or a globally distributed cluster — and jumping to architecture without doing the math is the fastest way to over-engineer or under-design.

**Back-of-envelope estimation** isn't about precision — it's about feasibility. You're trying to determine whether your design is in the right ballpark, not calculate exact server counts. Getting within 2–5× of the real number is perfectly useful. Getting the order of magnitude wrong (thinking you need 10 servers when you need 1,000) leads to architectures that collapse under real traffic.

The skill has three parts: knowing the **reference numbers** (how fast is a network call? how much data fits on a disk?), having a **systematic framework** (QPS → storage → bandwidth → memory → servers), and being comfortable with **rough math** in your head (round everything, use powers of 2 and 10, verify order of magnitude).

sections.title: The Reference Numbers Every Engineer Should Know
sections.content:
These numbers don't need to be memorized exactly — knowing the order of magnitude is what matters. The table below covers the numbers that appear most frequently in system design interviews.

| Operation | Latency | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| L1 cache reference | ~1 ns | CPU-local, fastest possible |
| L2 cache reference | ~4 ns | Still on-chip |
| Main memory (RAM) | ~100 ns | ~100× slower than L1 |
| SSD random read | ~100 μs | ~1,000× slower than RAM |
| HDD random read | ~10 ms | ~100× slower than SSD |
| Same-datacenter round trip | ~0.5 ms | Network within one DC |
| Cross-region round trip | ~50–150 ms | US East ↔ EU West |

| Resource | Capacity |
|---|---|
| Single HDD | ~10 TB |
| Single SSD | ~1–4 TB |
| Single server RAM | ~256–768 GB |
| Network bandwidth (1 Gbps) | ~100 MB/s useful throughput |
| QPS per web server (Spring Boot) | ~5,000–20,000 (depends on work per request) |
| QPS per PostgreSQL | ~10,000–50,000 (depends on query complexity) |
| QPS per Redis | ~100,000+ (simple operations) |

The critical insight: **RAM is 1,000× faster than SSD, SSD is 100× faster than HDD, and network calls are 5,000× slower than RAM**. Every architectural decision that moves data closer to the CPU (caching) or avoids network calls (colocation) is working with these ratios.

sections.title: The Five-Step Estimation Framework
sections.content:
Apply this framework to any system design problem. The steps build on each other — each answer feeds the next calculation.

**Step 1 — QPS (Queries Per Second):**
Start with daily active users or daily volume, then derive per-second load. Always calculate both **average and peak**.

Example: "10 million tweets per day" → `10M ÷ 86,400 ≈ 115 tweets/sec average`. Peak is typically 3–10× average → **350–1,150 tweets/sec at peak**. Read-heavy system? Multiply by read-to-write ratio. 100:1 means **11,500–115,000 reads/sec**.

**Step 2 — Storage:**
Estimate per-object size × volume × retention period. A tweet: 280 chars text (~300 bytes) + metadata (~200 bytes) + media pointer (~100 bytes) ≈ **600 bytes**. 10M tweets/day × 600 bytes = **6 GB/day** → **2.2 TB/year** → **11 TB over 5 years** (fits on 2 HDDs).

**Step 3 — Bandwidth:**
QPS × average response size. If each tweet read returns 2 KB (text + metadata + user info): 115,000 reads/sec × 2 KB = **230 MB/sec** → needs ~2.5 Gbps outbound bandwidth.

**Step 4 — Memory (Cache sizing):**
Follow the 80/20 rule — 20% of data generates 80% of traffic. Cache the hot 20%: 10M tweets/day × 0.2 × 600 bytes × 7 days ≈ **8.4 GB** → fits easily in one Redis instance.

**Step 5 — Server count:**
Divide peak QPS by per-server capacity. If each Spring Boot server handles 10K req/sec: 115,000 reads/sec ÷ 10,000 = **12 servers** (round up, add buffer for failover → **15 servers**).

sections.title: The Trap: Precision Over Judgment
sections.content:
The biggest mistake in estimation isn't getting a number wrong — it's **spending too long on precise math instead of reaching a conclusion**. The interviewer wants to see that you can quickly determine feasibility, not that you can do long division.

**Round aggressively.** Use 100,000 instead of 86,400 seconds/day (the error is ~15%, which is irrelevant at this scale). Use powers of 2 for memory (1 KB = 1,000 bytes, not 1,024). Multiply before dividing to avoid small fractions.

**State your assumptions explicitly.** "I'm assuming 100:1 read-to-write ratio" or "I'll estimate average tweet size at 600 bytes including metadata." The interviewer cares about your reasoning process, not the exact numbers. Wrong assumptions with clear reasoning are better than correct numbers with no explanation.

**Verify the order of magnitude.** After calculating, ask: does this make sense? 12 servers for a Twitter-scale read path sounds reasonable. 1,200 servers would suggest something is wrong. 1 server would suggest you underestimated traffic. This gut check is the most valuable part of estimation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Daily active users × actions/day ÷ 86,400 = QPS baseline** — always start with this; then multiply by 2–3 for peak.
- **Storage math: QPS × message size × seconds/day × retention days** — state the assumptions explicitly.
- **1 million req/day ≈ 12 req/sec; 1 billion ≈ 12K req/sec** — memorize these anchor points.
- **Network throughput ceiling: 1–10 Gbps per commodity server** — at 10KB payload × 10K req/sec = 100MB/sec = 800Mbps; one server handles it.
- **The estimation IS the requirement gathering** — declaring "100ms read latency" and "99.9% availability" directly determines your architecture choices.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation is the first thing interviewers evaluate in a system design session because it determines whether the architecture you propose is even in the right ballpark. The goal is not precision — it's establishing the order of magnitude that drives every subsequent component decision.

**The estimation framework:**
- Start with daily active users and their primary action: users × actions/day ÷ 86,400 seconds = average QPS; multiply by 2–3× for peak traffic
- Memorize the anchors: 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 req/sec; 1 billion ≈ 12K req/sec; these let you classify a system instantly as low/medium/high scale
- Storage: QPS × message size × seconds/day × retention days; state every assumption explicitly — interviewers score the reasoning process, not the precise number

**What the numbers tell you about architecture:**
- QPS determines server count: one application server handles ~1K–10K req/sec depending on work type; at 50K req/sec you need 10–50 servers and a real load balancer
- Storage growth determines whether you need time-series partitioning, tiered storage, or a columnar format for analytics
- Read-to-write ratio determines whether you need caching, read replicas, or both: a 100:1 read/write ratio is the classic caching candidate

**The two common errors:**
- Forgetting to multiply by peak traffic: average QPS is not the design point; size for 3× peak or you'll be paged on the first traffic spike
- Estimating storage without compression: Kafka messages compressed with LZ4 are 4–6× smaller than raw; PostgreSQL with TOAST handles large columns transparently

I recommend spending the first 5 minutes of any system design interview on this estimation — it signals engineering maturity and anchors every component decision to actual requirements.
